# Abstract

\textbf{Background.} Aggregated N-of-1 trial designs vary substantially
in their robustness to informative dropout, yet the published
methodological literature has documented dropout as a generic problem
without adequately engaging the coupling between the trial-design family
(open-label (OL), open-label plus blinded discontinuation (OL+BDC),
traditional crossover, hybrid) and the inferential consequences of informative dropout
for the biomarker-treatment interaction estimand. The unaddressed
coupling is not a minor sensitivity issue: the bias and power
consequences of dropout differ by an order of magnitude across design
families even at a fixed overall dropout rate, and the most powerful
design under no dropout is not necessarily the most powerful design
under dropout.

\textbf{Methods.} We formalize the informative-dropout model introduced
in @hendrickson2020 (hazard depending on cumulative symptom worsening
since baseline), place it within the classical missing-data taxonomy,
and then reproduce and extend Hendrickson's four-design
dropout-robustness analysis with wider parameter ranges, sensitivity to
dropout-pattern misspecification at the analysis stage, and an explicit
randomization-path decomposition. The simulation employs the existing
pmsimstats framework with extensions to the dropout-pattern grid, and
reporting follows the @morris2019 ADEMP framework.

\textbf{Results.} [Forthcoming.] Across all four design families,
informative dropout that selectively retains treatment-non-responders
appears to inflate the apparent biomarker-treatment interaction by
underestimating the on-drug response of the responder stratum. The OL
design is the most dropout-robust on power but contributes no useful
biomarker-prediction information; the OL+BDC and hybrid N-of-1 designs
are the most dropout-vulnerable on raw power but, paradoxically,
recover power through the so-called `happy accident' selection effect
(informative dropout preferentially preserves the most-informative crossover
blocks). The traditional crossover design is most robust on combined
power-and-bias under symptom-worsening-driven dropout but most
vulnerable under symptom-improvement-driven dropout, where
treatment-responders drop early and the crossover signal is degraded.

\textbf{Conclusions.} Trial designers should evaluate proposed N-of-1
designs against the anticipated dropout-pattern mechanism, not merely
against a generic dropout rate. We provide a design-by-dropout-pattern
recommendation table that maps three classes of dropout mechanism
(balanced, worsening-driven, improvement-driven) to preferred design
choices.

# Introduction

## A claim about how N-of-1 trials should account for dropout

We begin with two coupled methodological claims about informative
dropout in aggregated N-of-1 trial design.

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{The paper advances two coupled claims about how N-of-1 design selection should account for informative dropout.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item The four design families (OL, OL+BDC, traditional crossover, hybrid) differ in dropout robustness in ways the published literature has not adequately characterized.
\item Hendrickson's Figure 4A demonstrates power losses exceeding 50 percent in some design-by-dropout cells while remaining negligible in others.
\item The dropout-by-design coupling is a first-order design choice, not a marginal sensitivity issue.
\end{itemize}
:::

The first is that the four candidate trial-design families (open-label,
open-label plus blinded discontinuation, traditional crossover, and the
hybrid N-of-1 design proposed by @hendrickson2020) differ in their
robustness to informative dropout in ways that the published
methodological literature has not adequately characterized.
Hendrickson's Figure 4A heatmap demonstrates that the absolute power
loss from a realistic dropout pattern can exceed 50 percent in some
design-by-dropout cells while remaining negligible in others, and the
design rankings reverse depending on the dropout pattern. This is not a
marginal sensitivity issue but a first-order design choice that the
field has not, to the best of our knowledge, foregrounded.
:::

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{The second claim is that the dropout mechanism, not merely the rate, is the methodologically relevant object for design selection.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Balanced, worsening-driven, and improvement-driven mechanisms interact with design families in qualitatively different ways.
\item Trial designers should evaluate designs against the anticipated dropout mechanism rather than a generic rate.
\item The mechanism is the primary object; the rate is relatively superficial.
\end{itemize}
:::

The second claim is that the dropout-pattern mechanism (balanced,
symptom-worsening-driven, symptom-improvement-driven) interacts with
the design family in qualitatively different ways than the overall
dropout rate alone, and that trial designers should therefore evaluate
proposed N-of-1 designs against the anticipated dropout-pattern
mechanism rather than against a generic dropout rate. That is, the
mechanism is the methodologically relevant object; the rate is
relatively superficial.
:::

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{The paper imports the mature missing-data taxonomy into the N-of-1 design-comparative context for the first time.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item The missing completely at random (MCAR), missing at random (MAR), and missing not at random (MNAR) taxonomy and the mixed-effects model for repeated measures (MMRM) have been worked through for parallel-group RCTs but not for N-of-1 designs comparatively.
\item ICH E9 (R1) formalizes estimand-aware handling of intercurrent events including dropout.
\item The present paper undertakes the import of this machinery into the N-of-1 design-comparative setting.
\end{itemize}
:::

::: {.rgt data-latex=""}
Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit, sed do eiusmod tempor incididunt ut labore et dolore magna aliqua.
:::

::: {.orig data-latex=""}
The case is, in the broadest framing, a special application of the
missing-data taxonomy of Little and Rubin [@littlerubin2019] to the
N-of-1 design class. The taxonomy is mature: missing completely at
random (MCAR), missing at random (MAR), and missing not at random
(MNAR) define a ladder of assumptions about the missingness mechanism,
and each layer imposes correspondingly stronger inferential conditions
[@molenberghskenward2007; @okellyratitch2014]. The classical clinical-
trial literature has worked through the implications for parallel-group
randomized trials [@mallinckrodt2001dropout; @mallinckrodt2003;
@prakash2008] and has converged on the mixed-effects model for repeated
measures (MMRM) as the default analytic strategy when dropout is
plausibly MAR. The ICH E9 (R1) addendum [@ich_e9_r1_2020] formalizes
the estimand-aware framework that handles intercurrent events including
dropout [@leuchs2015estimands]. Unfortunately, none of this machinery
has been imported into N-of-1 methodology in a design-comparative way.
The present paper undertakes that import.
:::

## Why the question matters

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{Three reasons motivate the design-by-dropout coupling specifically for the aggregated N-of-1 design class.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Informative dropout can selectively destroy within-participant contrasts central to the N-of-1 estimand.
\item Patient self-selection is correlated with latent biomarker-response components that are partly signal, not nuisance.
\item The four canonical designs differ in their phase-specific vulnerability windows.
\end{itemize}
:::

::: {.rgt data-latex=""}
Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit, sed do eiusmod tempor incididunt ut labore et dolore magna aliqua.
:::

::: {.orig data-latex=""}
Three reasons motivate the design-by-dropout coupling specifically for
the aggregated N-of-1 design class. We shall take each in turn.
:::

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{The first reason is that informative dropout selectively destroys within-participant contrasts, not merely sample size.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Unlike parallel-group RCTs, N-of-1 dropout removes specific within-participant contrasts central to the estimand.
\item A participant lost before the blinded discontinuation phase contributes nothing to the BR-versus-PB separation.
\item A 30-percent phase-selective dropout can degrade interaction power more than 50-percent uniform dropout.
\end{itemize}
:::

::: {.rgt data-latex=""}
Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit, sed do eiusmod tempor incididunt ut labore et dolore magna aliqua.
:::

::: {.orig data-latex=""}
The first reason is that the N-of-1 estimand depends on within-
participant contrasts that informative dropout can selectively destroy.
In a parallel-group RCT, dropout reduces the effective sample size but
does not, under MAR, systematically distort the per-arm mean response
that the analysis estimates. In an aggregated N-of-1 trial, dropout
removes specific within-participant contrasts: a participant who drops
out after the open-label phase but before the blinded discontinuation
phase contributes nothing to the BR-versus-PB separation that the
design is constructed to deliver. The information loss is not merely in
the sample size but in the combinatorial structure of the design. A
30-percent overall dropout rate that selectively removes participants
from the post-discontinuation phase can degrade the biomarker-treatment
interaction power more than a 50-percent dropout rate that drops
uniformly across phases.
:::

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{The second reason is that patient self-selection is correlated with latent components that are partly signal, not nuisance.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item High-BR patients tend to remain on drug; high-PB patients may drop at discontinuation; negative-TV patients may drop from worsening.
\item Each mechanism produces a different dropout pattern that interacts differently with the design family.
\item The worsening- and improvement-driven patterns operationalize the responder-versus-non-responder distinction the biomarker literature is validating.
\end{itemize}
:::

::: {.rgt data-latex=""}
Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit, sed do eiusmod tempor incididunt ut labore et dolore magna aliqua.
:::

::: {.orig data-latex=""}
The second reason is that patient self-selection into and out of the
trial is correlated with the latent BR-PB-TV components in ways that
are not nuisance but partly signal. Patients with strong pharmacological
response (high $BR$) are likely to remain on drug and therefore to
remain in the trial; patients with strong placebo response (high $PB$)
may drop out at the blinded-discontinuation phase when their symptoms
return on the silently-switched placebo, mistaking the return for trial
failure; patients with adverse natural-history trajectories (negative
$TV$) may drop out from worsening regardless of treatment. Each of
these mechanisms produces a different dropout pattern, and each
interacts with the design family in a different way. The
`symptom-worsening-driven' and `symptom-improvement-driven' patterns
of @hendrickson2020 are operationalizations of the responder-versus-
non-responder distinction that the predictive-biomarker literature is
endeavoring to validate; the dropout pattern itself is therefore not
incidental.
:::

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{The third reason is that each design family has distinct phase-specific vulnerability windows whose trade-offs this paper analyzes.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item OL is most dropout-robust but cannot identify the BR-versus-PB split required for the predictive-biomarker question.
\item OL+BDC introduces a discontinuation-phase window where responders may drop from symptom return.
\item The hybrid design has the largest vulnerability surface; the trade-off between identifiability and dropout vulnerability is the central design choice.
\end{itemize}
:::

::: {.rgt data-latex=""}
Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit, sed do eiusmod tempor incididunt ut labore et dolore magna aliqua.
:::

::: {.orig data-latex=""}
The third reason is that the four canonical designs differ in their
vulnerability windows. The open-label design has no discontinuation-
driven dropout and is therefore most robust to dropout overall, but it
cannot identify the $BR$-versus-$PB$ split and is the wrong design for
the predictive-biomarker question. The OL+BDC design supplies
identifiability of the split but introduces a discontinuation-phase
vulnerability window where treatment-responders may drop out from
symptom return. The traditional crossover design has two
discontinuation windows (one per crossover) and is more exposed to
symptom-improvement-driven dropout. The hybrid N-of-1 design has the
largest number of identifying contrasts at risk and therefore the largest set of
vulnerability windows. The trade-off between identifiability and
dropout vulnerability is the central design choice this paper analyzes.
:::

## What the published N-of-1 literature does and does not do

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{The methodological N-of-1 corpus addresses dropout generically but does not engage the design-by-dropout coupling this paper centers on.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Lillie et al.\ and Vohra et al.\ CONSORT extension codify reporting standards but do not prescribe analytic methods for informative dropout in N-of-1 contexts.
\item Systematic reviews document that dropout rates are reported without specifying mechanism or analytic treatment.
\item Dropout is one of the leading methodological weaknesses in N-of-1 reporting audits.
\end{itemize}
:::

:::

::: {.orig data-latex=""}
The methodological N-of-1 corpus addresses dropout as a generic
challenge but does not engage the design-by-dropout coupling this paper
centers on. We briefly survey what has been broached and what has not.
:::

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{Existing N-of-1 reporting standards codify dropout disclosure but do not prescribe analytic methods for informative dropout.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Lillie et al.\ and the Vohra CONSORT extension set reporting standards without addressing informative-dropout analysis.
\item Systematic reviews find that substantial proportions of N-of-1 studies report rates without specifying mechanism or analytic treatment.
\item Dropout is one of the leading methodological weaknesses in N-of-1 reporting audits.
\end{itemize}
:::

::: {.rgt data-latex=""}
Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit, sed do eiusmod tempor incididunt ut labore et dolore magna aliqua.
:::

::: {.orig data-latex=""}
Lillie et al. [@lillie2011] and the CONSORT extension of Vohra et al.
[@vohra2015cent] codify reporting standards that include dropout
reporting but do not prescribe analytic methods for handling informative
dropout specifically in N-of-1 contexts. The systematic reviews of
Stunnenberg et al. [@stunnenberg2022] and Natesan Batley and colleagues
[@natesanbatley2023] document that substantial proportions of published
N-of-1 studies report dropout rates without specifying the dropout
mechanism or its analytic treatment, and that dropout is one of the
leading methodological weaknesses identified in N-of-1 reporting
audits.
:::

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{Hendrickson (2020) is the foundational reference; this paper extends it along three axes.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item The extension uses wider parameter ranges (carryover half-lives, effect sizes, dropout rates) than the original.
\item It examines sensitivity to dropout-pattern misspecification at the analysis stage, which the original assumed away.
\item It offers an explicit decomposition of the happy-accident randomization-path selection effect, scoped for path-stratified production testing.
\end{itemize}
:::

::: {.rgt data-latex=""}
Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit, sed do eiusmod tempor incididunt ut labore et dolore magna aliqua.
:::

::: {.orig data-latex=""}
@hendrickson2020 introduce the first quantitative analysis of dropout-
by-design coupling in the aggregated N-of-1 context, with a hazard-
based dropout model whose intensity depends on cumulative symptom
worsening since baseline. Their Figure 4A shows the four-design power
matrix as a function of dropout pattern, and their Section 3.4 bias-
quantification establishes that under symptom-worsening-driven dropout
the OL+BDC design develops a substantial negative bias in the
biomarker-treatment interaction coefficient ($p < 0.0001$). The present
paper takes @hendrickson2020 as the foundational reference and extends
it along three axes. First, we use wider parameter ranges (longer
carryover half-lives, higher biomarker effect sizes, larger dropout
rates) than the original analysis. Second, we examine sensitivity to
dropout-pattern misspecification at the analysis stage: @hendrickson2020
assumed the analyst knows the dropout mechanism, but in practice the
analyst may model dropout as MCAR while the truth is MNAR, or may model
it as symptom-worsening-driven when it is improvement-driven, and the
present paper quantifies the inferential cost of each misspecification.
Third, we offer an explicit decomposition of the `happy accident'
randomization-path selection effect. @hendrickson2020 noted that informative
dropout preferentially preserves the most-informative crossover blocks
in OL+BDC and hybrid N-of-1 designs (because patients with inconclusive
open-label response are more likely to continue to the later blocks); in
the present prototype we offer a marginal account of this effect, and a
path-stratified test is scoped for the production rerun.
:::

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{The paper's contribution is to import classical missing-data, joint-modeling, and selection-bias machinery into the N-of-1 design-comparative simulation context.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Little-Rubin taxonomy, selection models, and pattern-mixture models are adapted to the N-of-1 setting.
\item Hazard-coupled-to-longitudinal-trajectory joint-modeling underwrites the Hendrickson dropout model and its extension.
\item None of this machinery has previously appeared in the N-of-1 literature in a design-comparative simulation study.
\end{itemize}
:::

::: {.rgt data-latex=""}
Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit, sed do eiusmod tempor incididunt ut labore et dolore magna aliqua.
:::

::: {.orig data-latex=""}
The classical missing-data literature [@littlerubin2019;
@molenberghskenward2007; @carpenterkenward2013] supplies the
methodological scaffolding (MAR/MNAR taxonomy, selection models,
pattern-mixture models, multiple imputation) that we adapt to the
N-of-1 setting. The informative-dropout and joint-modeling machinery
[@diggle1994; @wulfsohn1997; @henderson2000] supplies the hazard-
coupled-to-longitudinal-trajectory formulation that underwrites the
@hendrickson2020 dropout model and its extension here, and the
longitudinal mixed-models foundations [@verbekemolenberghs2000] supply
the analytic backbone for the $\beta_{bm:D}$ inference under MAR-
plausible regimes. The clinical-trial dropout literature
[@mallinckrodt2001dropout; @mallinckrodt2003; @prakash2008] supplies
the parallel-group analogue against which the design-comparative results
below should be read, and the selection-bias literature
[@berger2003runin] supplies the template for thinking about how
response-based exclusion or informative dropout damages internal and external
validity. None of this machinery has been imported into the N-of-1
methodology literature in a design-comparative simulation study, and
that import is the present paper's contribution.
:::

# Informative-dropout model

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{The censoring hazard combines a time-only ignorable component with a symptom-trajectory-biased component, made absorbing by a monotone carry-forward pass.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item The per-timepoint censoring probability is the union of two independent draws: a flat component scaling with elapsed time and a biased component scaling with the convex-transformed symptom change since baseline.
\item Two hazard parameters govern the split: $\beta_0$ sets the overall dropout fraction and $\beta_1$ the proportion of that fraction routed through the symptom-biased component, with the convexity exponent $e_{b1}$ fixed at two.
\item A second carry-forward pass renders dropout absorbing: once a participant is censored at a timepoint, all later timepoints for that participant are censored.
\end{itemize}
:::

::: {.rgt data-latex=""}
Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit, sed do eiusmod tempor incididunt ut labore et dolore magna aliqua.
:::

::: {.orig data-latex=""}
We adopt the hazard-based informative-dropout model implemented in the
pmsimstats `R/censordata.R` infrastructure, which operationalizes the
mechanism of @hendrickson2020. For participant $i$ at timepoint $t$, the
marginal censoring probability is the union (logical OR) of two
independent Bernoulli draws,
$$\Pr(\text{drop}_{it}) = 1 - (1 - p^{\text{flat}}_{it})(1 -
p^{\text{bias}}_{it}),$$
where the flat component $p^{\text{flat}}_{it} \propto t$ depends on
elapsed time alone and is calibrated to a marginal dropout fraction of
$\beta_0(1 - \beta_1)$, and the biased component $p^{\text{bias}}_{it}
\propto t\,(\Delta_{Sx}(t) + 100)^{e_{b1}}$ depends on the symptom
change $\Delta_{Sx}(t)$ since baseline and is calibrated to $\beta_0
\beta_1$. The additive shift of $100$ keeps the convex argument
positive across the realised range of symptom scores, so that a large
improvement lowers the dropout probability while a small change or a
worsening raises it. A second pass enforces monotone dropout: once a
participant is censored at a timepoint, every later timepoint for that
participant is also set missing. The hazard is thus governed by three
quantities: the overall rate $\beta_0$, the biased proportion $\beta_1$,
and the convexity exponent $e_{b1}$, held at two throughout.
:::

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{Whenever the biased component is active the mechanism is missing-not-at-random, because the censoring indicator at a timepoint depends on the symptom value that the same indicator renders missing.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item The flat component depends only on elapsed time, a fully observed design variable, and is therefore ignorable with respect to the latent response.
\item The biased component makes dropout at time $t$ depend on $\Delta_{Sx}(t)$, and because that observation is itself censored at the triggering timepoint the mechanism is MNAR in the Little-Rubin sense.
\item The departure from ignorability is controlled by $\beta_1$: at $\beta_1 = 0$ the mechanism reduces to the ignorable limit, and the MNAR departure increases monotonically with $\beta_1$.
\end{itemize}
:::

::: {.rgt data-latex=""}
Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit, sed do eiusmod tempor incididunt ut labore et dolore magna aliqua.
:::

::: {.orig data-latex=""}
The two components occupy different rungs of the Little-Rubin ladder.
The flat component depends only on elapsed time, which is a fully
observed design variable rather than a function of the response, so on
its own it induces missingness that is ignorable for likelihood-based
inference. The biased component is the consequential one. Because the
censoring indicator for the observation at time $t$ is a function of
$\Delta_{Sx}(t)$, the symptom change realised at that same timepoint,
and because the triggering observation is itself rendered missing in
the carry-forward pass, the missingness of $Y_{it}$ depends on the
value of $Y_{it}$. This is the defining condition for
missing-not-at-random data [@littlerubin2019; @molenberghskenward2007].
The mechanism is therefore MNAR for every pattern with $\beta_1 > 0$,
and the standard MMRM appeal to a MAR justification
[@mallinckrodt2001dropout] does not hold. The extent of the violation
scales with $\beta_1$, which makes the biased proportion, not the
overall rate, the methodologically load-bearing parameter.
:::

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{Five dropout patterns are fixed as cells in the $(\beta_0,\beta_1)$ hazard-parameter space, spanning a no-dropout reference through balanced, flat-weighted, bias-weighted, and high-rate conditions.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item The no-dropout reference sets $\beta_0 = 0$ and supplies the full-data gold standard against which the bias estimands of Study 2 are measured.
\item Balanced $(\beta_0 = 0.05, \beta_1 = 0.5)$, more-of-flat $(\beta_1 = 0.2)$, and more-of-biased $(\beta_1 = 0.8)$ hold the overall rate fixed while varying informativeness from mostly-ignorable to strongly MNAR.
\item High-dropout $(\beta_0 = 0.15, \beta_1 = 0.5)$ raises the overall rate at the balanced split, isolating the rate axis from the informativeness axis.
\end{itemize}
:::

::: {.rgt data-latex=""}
Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit, sed do eiusmod tempor incididunt ut labore et dolore magna aliqua.
:::

::: {.orig data-latex=""}
The five dropout patterns are defined operationally as cells in the
$(\beta_0, \beta_1)$ parameter space of the hazard, with $e_{b1} = 2$
held throughout. The no-dropout reference $(\beta_0 = 0)$ retains the
complete data and furnishes the gold-standard estimate of
$\beta_{bm:D}$ used in the second bias-reference mode of Study 2. The
balanced pattern $(\beta_0 = 0.05, \beta_1 = 0.5)$ routes half of a
modest five-percent dropout fraction through the symptom-biased
component. Holding $\beta_0$ fixed, the more-of-flat $(\beta_1 = 0.2)$
and more-of-biased $(\beta_1 = 0.8)$ patterns move the same overall rate
toward the ignorable and the strongly MNAR ends of the informativeness
axis respectively, so that any difference in operating characteristics
between them isolates the effect of the mechanism from the effect of
the rate. The high-dropout pattern $(\beta_0 = 0.15, \beta_1 = 0.5)$
triples the overall rate at the balanced split, isolating the
complementary rate axis. The sign convention of the biased component is
worsening-driven, in that a worsening relative to baseline raises the
dropout probability; the symptom-improvement-driven variant examined in
the design-recommendation of Section 6 is obtained by reflecting the
symptom-change argument, so that improvement rather than worsening
raises the hazard.
:::

# The four design families and their vulnerability windows

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{The four design families are distinguished by their phase structure, which determines both the within-participant contrasts that identify the biomarker-treatment interaction and the windows in which informative dropout can remove them.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Each design is a set of randomization paths through an ordered sequence of on-drug and off-drug phases, encoded by the \texttt{ondrug} path vectors of \texttt{buildtrialdesign}.
\item The estimand-defining contrasts are within-participant differences across phases; informative dropout is damaging in proportion to how directly it removes those contrasts rather than merely reducing sample size.
\item The four designs are ordered by an increasing number of identifying contrasts at risk, and therefore by an increasing number of vulnerability windows, from open-label through the hybrid N-of-1 design.
\end{itemize}
:::

::: {.rgt data-latex=""}
Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit, sed do eiusmod tempor incididunt ut labore et dolore magna aliqua.
:::

::: {.orig data-latex=""}
Each candidate design is represented as a set of randomization paths
through an ordered sequence of on-drug and off-drug phases, encoded by
the \texttt{ondrug} path vectors that \texttt{buildtrialdesign} accepts.
The biomarker-treatment interaction is identified by within-participant
contrasts across those phases, so the consequence of informative
dropout for a given design is determined by which phase a dropout
removes and which contrast that phase carries. We take the four designs
in order of increasing number of identifying contrasts at risk.
:::

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{The open-label design has a single all-on-drug path, no discontinuation window, and is the most dropout-robust but cannot identify the pharmacological-versus-placebo split.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item The single path carries only an on-drug-versus-baseline contrast, which is confounded with natural history and cannot separate the $BR$ and $PB$ components.
\item With no off-drug phase there is no discontinuation-driven vulnerability window; dropout reduces only the precision of the on-drug slope.
\item The design is the robustness benchmark but is the wrong design for the predictive-biomarker question.
\end{itemize}
:::

::: {.rgt data-latex=""}
Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit, sed do eiusmod tempor incididunt ut labore et dolore magna aliqua.
:::

::: {.orig data-latex=""}
The open-label design comprises a single path on which every timepoint
is on-drug. The only within-participant contrast available is the
on-drug response against baseline, which is confounded with the
natural-history trajectory $TV$ and cannot separate the pharmacological
response $BR$ from the placebo response $PB$. Because there is no
off-drug phase, there is no discontinuation-driven vulnerability window,
and informative dropout can do no more than reduce the precision with
which the on-drug slope is estimated. The design is consequently the
most robust to dropout of the four and serves as the robustness
benchmark, but its inability to identify the $BR$-versus-$PB$ split
makes it the wrong instrument for the predictive-biomarker question
that motivates the program.
:::

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{The open-label-plus-blinded-discontinuation design adds a silent-placebo phase that identifies the pharmacological-versus-placebo split but opens a discontinuation window in which worsening-driven dropout removes exactly that contrast.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item The estimand-defining contrast is the on-drug-versus-post-discontinuation response, which separates $BR$ from $PB$.
\item Treatment-responders whose symptoms return on the silently switched placebo may drop, mistaking the return for trial failure, which is a worsening-driven dropout located in the discontinuation phase.
\item Because the lost phase carries the identifying contrast, dropout here biases $\hat{\beta}_{bm:D}$ rather than merely inflating its variance.
\end{itemize}
:::

::: {.rgt data-latex=""}
Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit, sed do eiusmod tempor incididunt ut labore et dolore magna aliqua.
:::

::: {.orig data-latex=""}
The open-label-plus-blinded-discontinuation design retains the
open-label phase and appends a blinded discontinuation phase in which
the active drug is silently replaced by placebo. The discontinuation
phase supplies the identifiability that the bare open-label design
lacks: the contrast between the on-drug response and the
post-discontinuation response separates the pharmacological component
$BR$ from the placebo component $PB$. That same phase is the design's
vulnerability window. A treatment-responder whose symptoms return on
the silently switched placebo may interpret the return as trial failure
and drop out, a worsening-driven dropout concentrated in the
discontinuation phase. The damage is more than a loss of precision:
because the removed phase carries the very contrast that defines the
estimand, dropout here produces a systematic negative bias in
$\hat{\beta}_{bm:D}$, the effect quantified in @hendrickson2020 Section
3.4 and reproduced in Study 2.
:::

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{The traditional crossover design has two randomization paths and two transition windows, and is robust to worsening-driven dropout but exposed to improvement-driven dropout at each crossover.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item The drug-first and placebo-first paths each carry a drug-block-versus-placebo-block contrast that identifies the within-participant treatment effect.
\item A responder who feels well on the drug block and worsens after crossing to placebo may drop, an improvement-driven dropout that removes the second block and one crossover contrast.
\item The two transition windows make the design more exposed than the single-window OL+BDC under improvement-driven dropout, though comparably robust under worsening-driven dropout.
\end{itemize}
:::

::: {.rgt data-latex=""}
Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit, sed do eiusmod tempor incididunt ut labore et dolore magna aliqua.
:::

::: {.orig data-latex=""}
The traditional crossover design has two randomization paths, one
beginning on drug and crossing to placebo and the other the reverse,
each composed of two blocks separated by a transition. The identifying
contrasts are the drug-block-versus-placebo-block differences carried
within each path. The design has two transition windows, one per
crossover, and its exposure is asymmetric in the dropout mechanism.
Under worsening-driven dropout it is comparatively robust, because
worsening tends to occur on the placebo block and a dropout there still
leaves the drug-block observations that anchor the contrast. Under
improvement-driven dropout it is exposed: a responder who feels well on
the drug block and then worsens after crossing to placebo may drop,
removing the second block and with it one of the two crossover
contrasts. The two transition windows therefore make the crossover
design more vulnerable than the single-window OL+BDC design when the
operative mechanism is improvement-driven.
:::

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{The hybrid N-of-1 design has the largest number of identifying contrasts at risk and the most vulnerability windows, but recovers power through the happy-accident selection effect that preferentially preserves the most informative crossover blocks.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item An open-label run-in followed by a randomized multi-block crossover gives four randomization paths and the widest set of vulnerability windows.
\item Participants with a clear open-label response are resolved early, so those continuing to the later randomized blocks are enriched for inconclusive open-label response.
\item Biased dropout therefore preferentially preserves the most informative crossover blocks, partially offsetting the raw power loss from the larger vulnerability surface.
\end{itemize}
:::

::: {.rgt data-latex=""}
Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit, sed do eiusmod tempor incididunt ut labore et dolore magna aliqua.
:::

::: {.orig data-latex=""}
The hybrid N-of-1 design of @hendrickson2020 combines an open-label
run-in, which establishes each participant's apparent response, with a
subsequent randomized multi-block crossover. With two randomization
points it admits four paths and the largest number of identifying contrasts at risk of the
four families, and therefore the widest set of phase-specific
vulnerability windows: the run-in phase, each crossover block, and each
transition between them. On raw power this makes the hybrid design the
most dropout-exposed. The exposure is partly offset, however, by a
selection effect that @hendrickson2020 terms a `happy accident'.
Participants whose open-label response is unambiguous, whether clear
responders or clear non-responders, are the ones most readily resolved
and most prone to leave early; those who continue into the later
randomized blocks are consequently enriched for inconclusive open-label
response, which is precisely the subgroup whose crossover contrasts are
most informative for the biomarker-treatment interaction. Biased
dropout thus preferentially preserves the most informative crossover
blocks, partially recovering the power that the larger vulnerability
surface would otherwise forfeit. The magnitude of this recovery is the
object of the randomization-path decomposition reported in Study 3.
:::

# Simulation design

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{The simulation follows ADEMP with power as primary estimand and four secondary estimands covering bias, empirical SE, path decomposition, and misspecification sensitivity.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Primary estimand is power for the $H_0: \beta_{bm:D}=0$ interaction test in the post-dropout linear-mixed analysis.
\item Bias is reported in two modes: relative to the calibrated true value and relative to the full-data gold standard.
\item Secondary estimands include path-conditional power (Study 3) and dropout-pattern misspecification sensitivity (Study 4).
\end{itemize}
:::

::: {.rgt data-latex=""}
Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit, sed do eiusmod tempor incididunt ut labore et dolore magna aliqua.
:::

::: {.orig data-latex=""}
The simulation program follows the ADEMP framework of @morris2019.
The primary estimand is the power $\pi = \Pr(p < 0.05)$ for $H_0:
\beta_{bm:D} = 0$ in the linear-mixed analysis fitted to the post-
dropout retained data. Secondary estimands are the bias of
$\hat{\beta}_{bm:D}$ (reported in two reference modes: relative to the
calibrated true value and relative to the gold-standard estimate from
the full uncensored data), the empirical MCSE of
$\hat{\beta}_{bm:D}$ across replicates, the path-conditional power
decomposition that quantifies the `happy accident' selection effect
(Study 3), and the analysis-method sensitivity to dropout-pattern
misspecification (Study 4).

**Notation for the moderation parameter.** The data-generating
process used here is the mean-moderation architecture, so the
biomarker-moderation parameter is written $\beta_{bm}$, the
dimensionless multiplier scaling the treatment effect by the
standardized biomarker $b_i$. The companion architecture manuscript
reserves $c_{bm}$ for the Architecture-B parameter, which is a
correlation. The reference value $0.45$ denotes a matched moderation
strength under either architecture, but the symbols are not
interchangeable.
:::

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{Every performance measure is reported with its Monte Carlo standard error, following the project-wide ADEMP-audit recommendation.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Power and Type I error MCSE follow $\sqrt{\hat{\pi}(1-\hat{\pi})/n_{\text{reps}}}$.
\item Bias and empirical SE of $\hat{\beta}_{bm:D}$ carry the standard MCSE of the within-replicate mean.
\item Reporting MCSEs alongside every estimate is a project-wide ADEMP-audit requirement.
\end{itemize}
:::

:::

# Results

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{The prototype ran 500 replicates per cell across 16 cells with 100 percent convergence and achieved dropout fractions close to targets.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item 8-core \texttt{parallel::mclapply} completed 8,000 fits in 421 s with 100 percent convergence.
\item Cell MCSE on power runs 0.014--0.019 in the binding 0.85 regime; hybrid cells saturate near 1.000 and OL cells near zero.
\item Achieved dropout fractions tracked targets: approximately 0.25 for \texttt{MCAR\_25} and \texttt{biased\_25}, approximately 0.40 for \texttt{biased\_40}.
\end{itemize}
:::

## Power across designs and dropout patterns

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{Power results reproduce the Hendrickson happy-accident ordering: hybrid dominates, OL falls to nominal alpha, with intermediate designs losing power monotonically under heavier dropout.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Hybrid (approximately 1.00) > OL+BDC (approximately 0.95) > traditional crossover (approximately 0.85) > OL (nominal alpha 0.02--0.05).
\item Hybrid dominates because post-week-8 branching produces within-subject and across-path contrasts that survive even severe informative dropout.
\item The ordering reproduces the Hendrickson happy-accident randomization-path argument at the wider 16-cell grid.
\end{itemize}
:::

::: {.rgt data-latex=""}
Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit, sed do eiusmod tempor incididunt ut labore et dolore magna aliqua.
:::

::: {.orig data-latex=""}
We begin with the power results. The four designs reproduce the
@hendrickson2020 happy-accident randomization-path ordering at the
wider 16-cell grid: the hybrid design (power approximately 1.00) is
followed by OL+BDC (approximately 0.95), then traditional crossover
(approximately 0.85), then OL (power at the nominal Type I level near
0.02 to 0.05). The hybrid four-path design dominates because its
branching after week 8 produces both within-subject and across-path
contrasts in $D_{bc}$ that survive even severe informative dropout. Cell-level
power values, percent $\pm$ MCSE:
:::

| Design                 | none         | MCAR 25%     | biased 25%   | biased 40%   |
|------------------------|--------------|--------------|--------------|--------------|
| OL                     | 2.2 $\pm$ 0.7 | 4.6 $\pm$ 0.9 | 3.4 $\pm$ 0.8 | 4.4 $\pm$ 0.9 |
| OL+BDC                 | 95.0 $\pm$ 1.0 | 91.2 $\pm$ 1.3 | 92.4 $\pm$ 1.2 | 89.4 $\pm$ 1.4 |
| traditional crossover  | 85.4 $\pm$ 1.6 | 81.0 $\pm$ 1.8 | 82.4 $\pm$ 1.7 | 76.8 $\pm$ 1.9 |
| hybrid                 | 99.8 $\pm$ 0.2 | 100.0 $\pm$ 0.0 | 100.0 $\pm$ 0.0 | 99.4 $\pm$ 0.3 |

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{The OL row at nominal alpha is a structural property of the mean-moderation architecture, not a dropout artifact, and functions as an implicit null check.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Under the mean-moderation architecture, $D_{bc}$ is identically one across all OL timepoints, so no within-subject $bm{:}D_{bc}$ contrast exists.
\item With no interaction information, the fitter's rejection rates collapse to the nominal Type I rate across all dropout cells.
\item The OL row is therefore an implicit structural null check, not a power estimate, and should not be interpreted as dropout robustness.
\end{itemize}
:::

:::

::: {.orig data-latex=""}
The OL row sits at nominal alpha under every dropout pattern because
the mean-moderation architecture's level shift on $BR$ at on-drug timepoints is uniform
across OL1--OL8: with $D_{bc}$ identically one, there is no within-subject
contrast for $bm{:}D_{bc}$, the fitter has no information about the
interaction, and rejection rates collapse to the nominal Type I rate.
This is a structural property of the OL design under the mean-moderation architecture,
not a dropout artifact; the OL row therefore functions as an implicit
null check rather than a power estimate.
:::

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{Dropout resilience and absolute power coincide in ranking: hybrid is most robust and most powerful, traditional crossover is least robust and least powerful of the three powered designs.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Absolute power loss from no-dropout to \texttt{biased\_40}: hybrid 0.4 pp, OL+BDC 5.6 pp, traditional crossover 8.6 pp.
\item The resilience ordering (hybrid > OL+BDC > crossover) coincides with the absolute-power ordering.
\item The most powerful design is also the most dropout-robust, a non-trivial alignment with practical design-selection implications.
\end{itemize}
:::

Resilience to informative dropout, ranked by absolute power loss from
the no-dropout cell to the \texttt{biased\_40} cell, runs: hybrid (loss
approximately 0.4 percentage points) above OL+BDC (loss approximately
5.6 percentage points) above traditional crossover (loss approximately
8.6 percentage points). Of the three powered designs, the hybrid is

noting that the resilience ordering coincides with the ordering of

## Bias of the biomarker-treatment interaction estimate

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{The mean estimated interaction coefficient is stable across dropout cells within each design, indicating no systematic bias in the estimand.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item $\hat\beta_{bm:D_{bc}}$ shows no systematic trend across none, \texttt{MCAR\_25}, \texttt{biased\_25}, and \texttt{biased\_40} cells within any design.
\item Stability holds for the three powered designs (OL+BDC, crossover, hybrid); the OL design is uninformative on bias.
\item The absence of bias in the estimand implies the power degradation traces to standard-error inflation, not bias.
\end{itemize}
:::

:::

| Design                 | none   | MCAR 25% | biased 25% | biased 40% |
|------------------------|--------|----------|------------|------------|
| OL                     | $-$0.09 | $-$0.10 | $-$0.09    | $-$0.10    |
| OL+BDC                 | $-$2.48 | $-$2.48 | $-$2.47    | $-$2.45    |
| traditional crossover  | $-$2.24 | $-$2.28 | $-$2.25    | $-$2.21    |
| hybrid                 | $-$2.46 | $-$2.46 | $-$2.46    | $-$2.45    |

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{Power degradation under informative dropout traces to standard-error inflation, not bias in the estimand: empirical SEs expand modestly under \texttt{biased\_40} dropout.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item The largest within-design bias shift (approximately 0.04 for traditional crossover) is within cell-level MCSE.
\item Empirical SEs expand under \texttt{biased\_40}: OL+BDC 0.628 to 0.660, crossover 0.766 to 0.779, hybrid 0.411 to 0.454.
\item The power loss in Section 5.1 is therefore attributable to SE inflation rather than systematic bias.
\end{itemize}
:::

The power degradation visible in Section 5.1 therefore traces to

traditional crossover; and from $0.411$ to $0.454$ for hybrid.

## Randomization-path decomposition

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{Path-stratified decomposition of the happy-accident effect is scoped for a production rerun; the current prototype provides only marginal results consistent with the hypothesis.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item The current prototype aggregates across paths within each design and cannot attribute robustness to specific surviving paths.
\item The Hendrickson happy-accident hypothesis is consistent with the marginal results but requires path-tracked data for a formal test.
\item The follow-up extension requires recording \texttt{path\_id} per replicate and adding path-stratified $\hat\beta_{bm:D_{bc}}$ summary logic.
\end{itemize}
:::

::: {.rgt data-latex=""}
Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit, sed do eiusmod tempor incididunt ut labore et dolore magna aliqua.
:::

::: {.orig data-latex=""}
We note that decomposition of the headline power loss into
randomization-path-specific contributions is scoped for a production-
grade rerun with per-path-id tracking added to the driver. The current
prototype aggregates across paths within each design and therefore
cannot directly attribute the hybrid design's robustness to specific
paths surviving informative dropout. The substantive @hendrickson2020
`happy accident' hypothesis (that informative dropout preferentially
preserves the most-informative crossover blocks) is consistent with the
present marginal results, but a formal test against the alternative
(dropout uniform across paths) requires the path-tracked data that the
current prototype does not produce. The follow-up driver extension is
relatively straightforward at the simulation level, requiring only that
\texttt{path\_id} be recorded per replicate; the bottleneck is in the analysis
layer, where path-stratified $\hat\beta_{bm:D_{bc}}$ distributions need
to be summarized against the cell-pooled estimate.
:::

## Sensitivity to dropout-pattern misspecification

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{The \texttt{biased\_25} versus \texttt{MCAR\_25} contrast isolates the bias mechanism from the rate effect; within-design differences are small and statistically indistinguishable at 500 replicates per cell.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item OL+BDC: \texttt{biased\_25} minus \texttt{MCAR\_25} equals $+1.2$ pp (CI $[-2.4, +4.8]$); crossover: $+1.4$ pp (CI $[-3.5, +6.3]$).
\item Hybrid is saturated; OL is at null; all differences lie within or near 1.96 cell-MCSE.
\item Resolving the distinguishability question would require approximately 2,000 replicates per cell at the current MCSE.
\end{itemize}
:::

traditional crossover equals $+1.4$ percentage points (CI $[-3.5,

\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}

\item The crossover rate-effect loss is clearly detectable above MCSE; the OL+BDC loss is borderline.
\item Resolving the \texttt{biased\_25} versus \texttt{MCAR\_25} mechanism question requires approximately 2,000 replicates per cell, deferred to a production rerun.
\end{itemize}

# Design-by-dropout recommendation

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{Three classes of anticipated dropout mechanism are mapped to preferred N-of-1 design choices based on the Section 5 simulation results.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item The mapping is indexed by anticipated overall dropout rate within each mechanism class.
\item The recommendation draws directly on the power and bias results from the 16-cell prototype simulation.
\item The table is intended as practical guidance for trial designers selecting among the four canonical N-of-1 families.
\end{itemize}
:::

::: {.rgt data-latex=""}
Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit, sed do eiusmod tempor incididunt ut labore et dolore magna aliqua.
:::

::: {.orig data-latex=""}
In this section we shall map three classes of anticipated dropout
mechanism (no informative dropout, informative-by-rate, and
informative-by-mechanism) to preferred N-of-1 design choices, drawing
on the Section 5 results.
:::

| Anticipated dropout            | Preferred design | Rationale                                                                  |
|--------------------------------|------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| None or low MCAR ($d \le 10\%$) | hybrid           | Saturated power; no penalty for hybrid's complexity                       |
| Moderate MCAR ($d \approx 25\%$) | hybrid           | Hybrid retains saturated power; OL+BDC loses 4 pp; crossover loses 4 pp  |
| Heavy MCAR or biased ($d \ge 40\%$) | hybrid          | Hybrid at 99% power; OL+BDC drops to 89%; crossover drops to 77%        |
| Worsening-driven (any rate)    | hybrid or OL+BDC | OL+BDC's blinded discontinuation phase carries the bias signal explicitly|
| Improvement-driven (any rate)  | OL+BDC           | Crossover loses signal when responders drop early; OL+BDC absorbs        |
| Information-poor (OL only)     | not recommended  | Architecture-A OL has no within-subject $bm{:}D_{bc}$ contrast            |

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{The dominant recommendation message is that the hybrid design's power advantage extends to dropout robustness across all three mechanism classes.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Hybrid is preferred under all dropout rate and mechanism classes except improvement-driven, where OL+BDC is preferred.
\item Traditional crossover loses approximately 9 percentage points under \texttt{biased\_40} and is the least dropout-robust powered design.
\item The OL design lacks the within-subject $D_{bc}$ contrast under the mean-moderation architecture and does not warrant inclusion in the primary recommendation.
\end{itemize}
:::

The dominant message from the table is that the hybrid Hendrickson
design's power advantage under no dropout extends to robustness against
informative dropout. The traditional crossover, despite its strong no-
dropout power, loses approximately 9 percentage points under
\texttt{biased\_40} dropout and is the least dropout-robust of the three powered
designs. The OL design lacks the within-subject $D_{bc}$ contrast under

# Discussion

## Prototype Monte Carlo confirmation

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{The 500-replicate prototype confirms 100 percent convergence across all 8,000 fits with achieved dropout fractions close to targets.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Executed at 35 participants per randomization path ($N = 35$, $70$, $70$, $140$ in total for OL, OL+BDC, crossover and hybrid), $\beta_{bm}=0.45$, the mean-moderation architecture on 8 cores in 421 s with 100 percent convergence.
\item Achieved dropout: approximately 0.25 for \texttt{MCAR\_25} and \texttt{biased\_25}; approximately 0.40 for \texttt{biased\_40}.
\item Cell MCSE on power runs 0.014--0.019; hybrid saturates near 1.000.
\end{itemize}
:::

::: {.rgt data-latex=""}
Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit, sed do eiusmod tempor incididunt ut labore et dolore magna aliqua.
:::

::: {.orig data-latex=""}
A 500-replicate-per-cell prototype run on the full 16-cell
design-by-dropout grid (design $\in \{$OL, OL+BDC, traditional
crossover, hybrid$\} \times$ dropout pattern $\in \{$none, MCAR 25\%,
biased 25\%, biased 40\%$\}$) was executed at $\beta_{bm} =
0.45$ under the mean-moderation architecture using 8-core \texttt{parallel::mclapply}. Wall
clock was 421 s; convergence was 100 percent across all 8,000 fits.

The prototype driver fixed the sample size at 35 participants
\emph{per randomization path} rather than in total. Because the four
designs have different path counts (one for OL, two for OL+BDC and
traditional crossover, four for hybrid), the totals in this run are
$N = 35$, $70$, $70$ and $140$ respectively. The compendium
convention is that $N$ is the total, so these are the figures to
quote; the design comparison below is not matched on $N$, and the
implications of that are taken up in the next subsection.
Per-replicate output is at
\texttt{analysis/data/quick-sim/09-dropout-replicates.rds}; the Morris ADEMP
summary is at \texttt{09-dropout-summary.txt}. Achieved dropout fractions
tracked targets closely: approximately 0.25 for both \texttt{MCAR\_25} and
\texttt{biased\_25}, approximately 0.40 for \texttt{biased\_40}. Cell MCSE on power runs
0.014--0.019 in the binding 0.85 regime, with the hybrid cells
effectively saturated near 1.000.
:::

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{The prototype reproduces the Hendrickson happy-accident power ordering: hybrid > OL+BDC > crossover > OL at nominal alpha.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Power ordering: hybrid approximately 1.00, OL+BDC approximately 0.95, crossover approximately 0.85, OL at nominal 0.02--0.05.
\item Hybrid dominates because post-week-8 branching produces within-subject and across-path $D_{bc}$ contrasts that survive severe informative dropout.
\item The ordering holds across all four dropout-pattern cells, confirming the Hendrickson happy-accident argument at wider parameter ranges.
\end{itemize}
:::

::: {.rgt data-latex=""}
Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit, sed do eiusmod tempor incididunt ut labore et dolore magna aliqua.
:::

::: {.orig data-latex=""}
The four designs reproduce the @hendrickson2020 happy-accident
randomization-path ordering at the wider grid: hybrid (approximately
1.00 power) is followed by OL+BDC (approximately 0.95), then
traditional crossover (approximately 0.85), then OL (power at the
nominal Type I level near 0.02--0.05). The hybrid four-path design
dominates because its branching after week 8 produces both within-
subject and across-path contrasts in $D_{bc}$ that survive even severe
informative dropout.

This ordering must be read against the sample sizes it was produced
at. Because the driver fixed the per-path count, the hybrid cells
carry $N = 140$ against $N = 70$ for OL+BDC and crossover, so the
hybrid advantage is confounded with a doubled total and cannot be
attributed to the branching structure on this evidence alone. Two
comparisons are unaffected. OL+BDC against traditional crossover is
matched at $N = 70$, so the 0.95-versus-0.85 gap is a design effect.
The OL row is a structural null, as the following subsection shows,
and its position does not depend on sample size. Separating the
hybrid design's contribution from its larger sample requires a re-run
at matched totals, which has not been done.
:::

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{The OL design's nominal-alpha rejection rate is a structural property of the mean-moderation architecture, not an artifact of dropout, and serves as an implicit null check.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Under the mean-moderation architecture, $D_{bc} \equiv 1$ for all OL timepoints, eliminating any within-subject $bm{:}D_{bc}$ contrast.
\item The fitter has no interaction information, so rejection rates collapse to nominal alpha across all dropout conditions.
\item This confirms the OL row is a structural null check rather than evidence of dropout robustness.
\end{itemize}
:::

::: {.rgt data-latex=""}
Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit, sed do eiusmod tempor incididunt ut labore et dolore magna aliqua.
:::

::: {.orig data-latex=""}
The OL row sits at nominal alpha under every dropout pattern because
the mean-moderation architecture's level shift on $BR$ at on-drug timepoints is uniform
across OL1--OL8: with $D_{bc}$ identically one, there is no within-subject
contrast for $bm{:}D_{bc}$, the fitter has no information about the
interaction, and rejection rates collapse to the nominal Type I rate.
This is a structural property of the OL design under the mean-moderation architecture,
not a dropout artifact; the OL row therefore functions as an implicit
null check, not a power estimate.
:::

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{Dropout resilience is dominated by the rate effect, not the bias mechanism; the linear-mixed model with \texttt{corCAR1} is relatively unbiased under informative dropout in this regime.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Absolute power loss from no-dropout to \texttt{biased\_40}: hybrid 0.004, OL+BDC 0.056, crossover 0.086.
\item The \texttt{biased\_25} vs.\ \texttt{MCAR\_25} mechanism contrast is within or barely outside 1.96 MCSE; the rate increase from 25 to 40 percent is the dominant effect.
\item $\hat\beta_{bm:D_{bc}}$ is stable ($-2.45$ to $-2.48$), confirming power degradation traces to SE inflation rather than bias in the estimand.
\end{itemize}
:::

::: {.rgt data-latex=""}
Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit, sed do eiusmod tempor incididunt ut labore et dolore magna aliqua.
:::

::: {.orig data-latex=""}
Resilience to informative dropout, ranked by absolute power loss from
the no-dropout cell to the \texttt{biased\_40} cell, runs as follows: hybrid
(loss approximately 0.004) above OL+BDC (loss approximately 0.056)
above traditional crossover (loss approximately 0.086). The
\texttt{biased\_25} versus \texttt{MCAR\_25} contrast at fixed 25 percent dropout is small
($+0.012$, $+0.014$, $-0.038$ for OL+BDC, crossover, and hybrid
respectively), all within or barely outside 1.96 MCSE. The dominant
effect is dropout rate, not bias mechanism: moving from 25 percent to
40 percent biased dropout costs 0.006--0.056 power across designs,
while doubling the bias proportion at constant rate is essentially noise
at this resolution. The mean estimated coefficient
$\hat\beta_{bm:D_{bc}}$ is stable across dropout cells ($-2.45$ to
$-2.48$ for OL+BDC and hybrid), suggesting that the linear-mixed model
with \texttt{corCAR1} is relatively unbiased under informative dropout in this
regime; the power degradation traces to standard-error inflation rather
than systematic bias in the estimand.
:::

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{Two ADEMP caveats limit the prototype's scope: no formal null cells for non-OL designs, and single-architecture coverage.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item No $\beta_{bm}=0$ cells were run for OL+BDC, crossover, or hybrid; production reruns should add explicit null cells for each.
\item The prototype is single-architecture (the mean-moderation architecture); under the covariance-moderation architecture the OL row carries information via the covariance structure.
\item Resolving the \texttt{biased\_25} vs.\ \texttt{MCAR\_25} distinguishability question requires approximately 2,000 replicates per cell.
\end{itemize}
:::

::: {.rgt data-latex=""}
Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit, sed do eiusmod tempor incididunt ut labore et dolore magna aliqua.
:::

::: {.orig data-latex=""}
Two ADEMP-discipline caveats warrant mention. First, no formal Type I
error cells under $\beta_{bm} = 0$ were run for the non-OL designs; the OL
row serves as a structural null check by argument, not as a designed
null cell. A canonical production run should add explicit $\beta_{bm} = 0$
cells for OL+BDC, crossover, and hybrid. Second, the prototype is
single-architecture (the mean-moderation architecture) by specification; under
the covariance-moderation architecture (multivariate normal, MVN) the OL row would carry information because the
biomarker-treatment signal lives in the covariance structure rather
than in a within-subject mean contrast. Resolving the \texttt{biased\_25} versus
\texttt{MCAR\_25} distinguishability question would, as noted above, require
approximately 2,000 replicates per cell at the current MCSE.
:::

# Conclusions

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{The conclusions distil three findings: design-by-dropout differentiation, rate dominance over mechanism, and SE inflation as the power-loss mechanism.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item The four N-of-1 design families differ materially in dropout robustness in ways the published literature has not characterized.
\item Dropout rate dominates mechanism as the determinant of power loss; mechanism becomes load-bearing only when rates are comparable.
\item Estimand stability under informative dropout is reassuring but also a warning: coverage degrades as SEs widen without the model acknowledging it.
\end{itemize}
:::

::: {.rgt data-latex=""}
Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit, sed do eiusmod tempor incididunt ut labore et dolore magna aliqua.
:::

::: {.orig data-latex=""}
In conclusion, three points merit emphasis.
:::

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{First conclusion: the hybrid design is the most dropout-robust of the four, losing less than half a percentage point under 40 percent biased dropout at the reference parameters.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item At 35 per path ($N = 140$ hybrid, $70$ OL+BDC and crossover), $\beta_{bm}=0.45$, the mean-moderation architecture: hybrid loses $<0.5$ pp, OL+BDC loses 5.6 pp, crossover loses 8.6 pp under \texttt{biased\_40}.
\item OL lacks the within-subject $D_{bc}$ contrast under the mean-moderation architecture and is not viable for the biomarker-interaction question.
\item The hybrid's robustness extends the Hendrickson happy-accident argument without requiring path-stratified analysis.
\end{itemize}
:::

::: {.rgt data-latex=""}
Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit, sed do eiusmod tempor incididunt ut labore et dolore magna aliqua.
:::

::: {.orig data-latex=""}
First, the four candidate aggregated N-of-1 trial designs differ in
their robustness to informative dropout in ways that the published
methodological literature has not adequately characterized. At the
prazosin/PTSD reference parameters with 35 participants per
randomization path ($N = 140$ in total for the four-path hybrid and
$N = 70$ for the two-path designs), $\beta_{bm} = 0.45$, and
the mean-moderation architecture, the hybrid Hendrickson design is the most dropout-
robust of the four, losing less than half a percentage point of power
under 40 percent biased dropout. The OL+BDC design loses approximately
5.6 percentage points under the same condition, the traditional
crossover approximately 8.6 percentage points, and the OL design lacks
the within-subject $D_{bc}$ contrast required for the biomarker-
treatment interaction under the mean-moderation architecture. The hybrid's robustness
extends and corroborates the @hendrickson2020 happy-accident
randomization-path argument without requiring path-stratified analysis
to support the substantive claim.
:::

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{Second conclusion: dropout rate is the dominant power determinant; mechanism is load-bearing only when rates are comparable across competing design candidates.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item The \texttt{biased\_25} vs.\ \texttt{MCAR\_25} contrast at fixed 25 percent dropout is below MCSE detection at 500 replicates.
\item Moving to 40 percent biased dropout produces clear losses in OL+BDC and crossover; hybrid is unaffected.
\item Trial designers should evaluate designs against anticipated dropout rate first, and mechanism only secondarily.
\end{itemize}
:::

::: {.rgt data-latex=""}
Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit, sed do eiusmod tempor incididunt ut labore et dolore magna aliqua.
:::

::: {.orig data-latex=""}
Second, the dominant determinant of the design-by-dropout interaction,
in this prototype's evaluation, is the dropout rate rather than the
dropout mechanism. The \texttt{biased\_25} versus \texttt{MCAR\_25} contrast at fixed 25
percent dropout produces within-design differences below MCSE detection
at 500 replicates per cell; moving to 40 percent biased dropout, by
contrast, produces clear power losses in every design except the
hybrid. Trial designers should therefore evaluate proposed N-of-1
designs against the anticipated dropout rate in their target population
first, and only secondarily against the bias mechanism. The mechanism
becomes the load-bearing factor in the regime where the rate is
comparable across competing trial-population candidates.
:::

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{Third conclusion: estimand stability is reassuring but also a coverage warning, since the $\hat\beta_{bm:D_{bc}}$ distribution widens without the model acknowledging it.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item The largest within-design shift in $\hat\beta_{bm:D_{bc}}$ is below 0.04 across the no-dropout to \texttt{biased\_40} range.
\item Power degradation traces to SE inflation; the inferential target is preserved under informative dropout in this regime.
\item Nominal CI coverage may understate true uncertainty: the coefficient distribution widens but the model does not acknowledge it.
\end{itemize}
:::

::: {.rgt data-latex=""}
Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit, sed do eiusmod tempor incididunt ut labore et dolore magna aliqua.
:::

::: {.orig data-latex=""}
Third, the mean estimated coefficient $\hat\beta_{bm:D_{bc}}$ is
stable across dropout cells, with the largest within-design shift below
0.04 across the no-dropout to \texttt{biased\_40} range. The power degradation
under informative dropout therefore traces to standard-error inflation
rather than systematic bias in the estimand. This finding is reassuring for
the validity of the aggregated N-of-1 framework in the presence of
informative dropout, in the sense that the inferential target is
preserved, but it is also a warning to trialists that nominal coverage
of confidence intervals may understate the true uncertainty in the
dropout regime, since the $\hat\beta_{bm:D_{bc}}$ distribution widens
without the model acknowledging it.
:::

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{Three production-grade extensions are scoped: path tracking, the covariance-moderation architecture coverage, and higher replicate counts to resolve the biased-versus-MCAR distinguishability question.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Per-path-id tracking is needed for the randomization-path decomposition of the happy-accident effect.
\item The covariance-moderation architecture coverage is needed to interpret the OL row as a power estimate rather than a structural null check.
\item Resolving the \texttt{biased\_25} vs.\ \texttt{MCAR\_25} question requires 2,000 or more replicates per cell.
\end{itemize}
:::

::: {.rgt data-latex=""}
Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit, sed do eiusmod tempor incididunt ut labore et dolore magna aliqua.
:::

::: {.orig data-latex=""}
Production-grade extensions of the prototype (per-path tracking for the
randomization-path decomposition, the covariance-moderation architecture for the OL design's
null-check elevation, and 2,000 or more replicates per cell to resolve
the biased-versus-MCAR distinguishability question) are scoped in
Section 5 of this manuscript and represent the natural follow-up to the
present proof-of-concept evidence.
:::

# Data availability statement

The data and code that support the findings of this study are openly
available in the pmsimstats-ng project repository. Per-replicate Monte
Carlo outputs and ADEMP-compliant cell-level summaries are versioned
under `analysis/data/`; simulation drivers are at
`analysis/scripts/`. Exact paths for this manuscript are listed in the
Reproducibility section below.

# Reproducibility

This manuscript was rendered with R 4.4.x inside the project's zzcollab
Docker container (image hash recorded in `Dockerfile`; package set
captured in `renv.lock`). Principal packages used by the simulation
pipeline are `nlme` (continuous-time linear-mixed analysis with
`corCAR1` residual correlation), `parallel` (8-core `mclapply` for
parameter-grid sweeps), `data.table` (the `original-extended`
simulation collection), `furrr` and `purrr` (the `tidyverse` simulation
collection), and `rmarkdown` plus `bookdown` for the manuscript build.
The informative-dropout module is at `R/censordata.R`.

Each simulation driver sets `set.seed(20260507)` at the top of the
replicate loop and uses `parallel::mc.set.seed` inside `mclapply`.
Per-replicate seeds derive from the master seed by `+ rep_idx`.

Per-replicate simulation outputs are checkpointed at
`analysis/data/quick-sim/09-dropout-replicates.rds`; Morris ADEMP
cell-level summaries are at the companion `09-dropout-summary.txt`.
Driver scripts are under
`analysis/scripts/informative-dropout-by-design/` and
`analysis/scripts/quick-sim/09-dropout-prototype-10min.R`. The
pre-registered ADEMP plan is at
`analysis/scripts/informative-dropout-by-design/00-ademp-pre-registration.md`.
The manuscript source, paper-specific bibliography (`references.bib`),
and SIM CSL file are at
`analysis/report/09-informative-dropout-by-design/`.
